1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4.name: Sicilian Defence
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4.strategy: Takes the pawn and trades a flank pawn for White's central one. Black gets the semi-open c-file and two central pawns against one, while White recaptures and gains a lead in development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6.name: Sicilian Defence: Modern Variations, Anti-Qxd4 Move Order
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4 before any exchange, so White has to defend it, and the knight on c3 that does so takes away the c-pawn's push for a clamp on d5. The price is that White gains an extra option of taking on c5, which leads to unclear, double-edged play.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight at once, but invites 4.d5: the knight has to retreat, and after the exchange on e5 White has a clear space advantage with pawns on d5 and e4 while Black has no Sicilian counterplay.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4.strategy: The natural recapture: the knight lands in the centre with access to b5 and f5. White has traded a central pawn for a flank pawn and gets easy development and open lines for both bishops.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.c3.name: Sicilian Defence: Modern Variations, Tartakower
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.c3.strategy: Leaves the pawn on d4 with Black and offers it for quick development, a delayed form of a pawn gambit. Because Black's d-pawn is already on d6, some of the usual ways of meeting it are closed; Black can also simply decline and White has given up the easy recapture.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4.name: Sicilian Defence: Chekhover Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4.strategy: Recaptures with the queen instead of the knight, but the queen stands in the centre where a knight can chase it, and White usually has to give up the bishop pair to avoid losing time. The lead in development is meant to make up for it.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6.name: Sicilian Defence: Modern Variations, Main Line
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6.strategy: Develops and attacks e4 at once, asking White how to defend it. With ...d6 already controlling e5, White cannot push the pawn, and the clamp with c4 fails because the pawn on e4 would be lost.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6.name: Sicilian Defence: Dragon Variation, Accelerated Dragon
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6.strategy: Fianchettoes at once, but does not attack e4. White can take space with c4 and clamp down on d5, which cramps Black's play.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight with an attack on d4 and keeps the choice of set-up open. Unlike ...Nf6, it does not force Nc3, so White can play c4 at once and clamp down on d5.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Defends e4 and develops a piece. White gets a flexible set-up with an eye on queenside castling, and Black now chooses the pawn structure and the kind of game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Prins Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Defends e4 with a pawn instead of a piece, so the c-pawn stays free to take space later. The cost is a loosened kingside, and Black's reply in the centre gains time against the knight.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Modern Variations, Ginsberg Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Apparently leaves e4 to its fate. If Black takes it, f7 comes under fire from the bishop and a queen coming to h5, and sacrifices on f7 expose the uncastled king. A tricky surprise, but not a move White can rely on.
Hits the knight at once and takes central space. White's knight has to move, and Black's pawns on e5 and d6 leave d5 as a hole that Black must watch.
Attacks the knight on d4 at once and develops. White can reply with c4, the clamp that 5.f3 was played for, which makes the ...d5 break hard for Black to achieve.
Heads for a fianchetto, but allows the clamp that 5.f3 aims for: with c4 White controls d5, and Black's central break becomes hard to achieve while the king's bishop gets a long diagonal to bite on.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Prins Variation, Venice Attack
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Checks first so that the knight can jump to f5 instead of retreating, where it hits d6 and g7. With f3 already guarding e4, White's centre is secure while the knight does the work, and this is the usual way to meet ...e5.
Retreats the knight to keep c4 available for the clamp on d5. But without the check Black frees the game at once with ...d5, hitting e4, and the knight on b3 does little.
A modest retreat that supports a later c4 and Nc3, but the knight blocks the king's bishop on e2 and White gives Black time to play ...d5 and open the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Najdorf Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..background: Players tried 5...a6 in the 1920s. It is named after Miguel Najdorf, who played it as early as 1937 but was not the first strong player to do so; the Czech master Karel Opočenský was among the first to combine 5...a6 with ...e5.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Takes b5 away from White's bishop and knights and prepares queenside expansion, while leaving the central set-up open. One of the most popular and most deeply studied systems against the open game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Classical Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Brings out the knight to its natural square and leaves the bishop's set-up for later. Black stays flexible, while White can choose between a sharp attack and calm development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Dragon Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..background: Fyodor Dus-Chotimirsky named it in 1901, noticing a resemblance between Black's kingside pawns on d6, e7, f7, g6 and h7 and the stars of the Draco constellation.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the bishop on the long diagonal, aiming at the queenside. In the sharpest lines White castles long and attacks the kingside while Black counterattacks on the queenside: an extremely sharp, complicated race.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Kupreichik Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..background: Named after Viktor Kupreichik, its most frequent proponent.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: A rare move that keeps the bishop ready to meet an exchange on b5 and can lead back to better-known set-ups. It avoids the main theory but spends a move on a bishop that no other main line needs.

Takes the centre at once, but the check on b5 follows and the exchange of light-squared bishops leaves the d5 square weak. White gets a knight outpost on f5 that Black can challenge only with concessions.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Najdorf Variation, English Attack
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..background: Called the English Attack because English grandmasters Murray Chandler, John Nunn and Nigel Short popularised it in the 1980s. It has become White's most popular weapon against the Najdorf.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: The modern main line, built for attack: White prepares to castle long and storm the kingside with pawns, while Black counters on the queenside. With the kings on opposite wings the game is a race in which every tempo counts, and both sides must know their theory.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Najdorf Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..background: Until the 1980s this was the more typical way to meet the Najdorf, before 6.Be3 became White's most popular move.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: The old main line: it threatens Bxf6, which would double Black's pawns, so Black has to react at once. White follows with sharp central and kingside play, Black seeks counterplay on the queenside, and the resulting positions are among the most heavily analysed in the opening.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Najdorf Variation, Opocensky Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..background: Efim Geller was an early proponent of this quiet move.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: The quiet, positional choice: White prepares to castle short and keeps e4 and the d5 square under control instead of rushing a kingside attack. The game becomes slower and more strategic, and Black is free to choose between a space-gaining and a compact central set-up.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Najdorf Variation, Amsterdam Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Takes control of e5 and opens the f-file for a kingside attack, usually with castling short. The price is a looser king position, in particular on the g1-a7 diagonal, which gives Black targets for queen counterplay.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Najdorf Variation, Lipnitsky Attack
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..background: Fischer developed its theory extensively, taking inspiration from Veniamin Sozin's 6.Bc4 against the Classical Sicilian. It was a frequent guest at the top level through the 1970s.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Aims the bishop at f7 and tries to seize the initiative with direct threats instead of slow build-up. Black can shut the diagonal at once, and the bishop on c4 then becomes a target for queenside pawn expansion, so White has to choose a plan with care.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Najdorf Variation, Zagreb Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: The Zagreb Variation fianchettoes the king's bishop to control d5 and the long diagonal, a calm positional plan far from the sharpest attacks. It is also meant to discourage Black's queenside expansion with ...b5.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Najdorf Variation, Adams Attack
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..background: Introduced by Weaver Adams in the middle of the twentieth century. It has mostly been used as a surprise weapon against the Najdorf.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: An odd-looking move with a plan: it takes g4 away from Black's pieces and prepares a kingside pawn advance. But it develops nothing, so Black gets time to claim the centre, and the move works best as a surprise weapon.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Najdorf Variation, Petronić Attack
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: The rook steps to g1 so that g4 can follow without losing the pawn, while the other rook stays free for castling long. It looks odd and costs a tempo, but it is not bad and has surprise value.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Najdorf Variation, Yates Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Develops the bishop on an awkward square: its own e4 pawn blocks one diagonal and it blocks the queen's file. It is not bad, only less purposeful than the other bishop moves, and Black gets time to set up the centre as it likes.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Najdorf Variation, Dekker Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Offers the g-pawn at once: Black wins it with 6...Nxg4 or 6...Bxg4, because the queen cannot recapture without being taken by the second piece. White hopes for attacking chances in return, but they do not make up for the pawn.

The standard answer: the pawn closes the bishop's diagonal to f7 and covers d5 and f5. Black accepts a slightly passive piece set-up for safety, and prepares ...b5 to chase the bishop and expand on the queenside.
Hits the undefended bishop along the c-file, so White has to move or defend it, but the queen does nothing about the pressure on f7. Black still has to close the diagonal with ...e6.
Develops the knight and eyes e5 and c5, but it blocks the c8-bishop and leaves f7 under pressure, so ...e6 is still needed.

Claims space in the centre and hits the d4 knight at once, keeping the pure Najdorf structure. The price is a backward d6 pawn and a weak d5 square, which White can use as an outpost; in return Black gets a solid centre against White's slower set-up.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Scheveningen Variation, Classical Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Heads for a compact set-up: the pawn guards d5 and f5, and the bishop can go to e7 so that Black castles early. It is a solid, less ambitious choice, and White can plan a kingside pawn advance, so Black must be ready for a fight over the centre.
Develops the knight and keeps both ...e5 and ...e6 for later, covering e5 and f6 solidly. The knight blocks the c8-bishop, so Black commits to a slower set-up.

The main reply: Black attacks the d4 knight at once and takes space in the centre. The price is the weak d5 square; once the knight retreats, Black has to show that piece play and queenside counterplay come faster than White's kingside attack.

Black builds a compact centre. Because the a-pawn has already moved, ...e5 answers an early g4 without Bb5+ in the way, which avoids the sharpest White line against a direct ...e6 on move five. Black accepts a solid but slightly passive game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Najdorf Variation, English Attack, Anti-English
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: The Anti-English: the knight attacks the e3 bishop to trade it off or force it back, because that bishop is the engine of White's attack. It is safe here since ...a6 has taken b5 away, unlike in lines where Bb5+ is available.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Najdorf Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: The main line: the e-pawn unblocks the queen's diagonal and prepares the bishop to e7, so the pin on the f6 knight can be broken. Black accepts a compact but slightly passive structure and looks for counterplay on the queenside.

Prepares to meet Bxf6 by recapturing with the knight, so Black's pawns stay intact, and keeps the e-pawn's options open. The knight on d7 blocks the c8-bishop and slows development, which lets White play for the initiative.

Develops with an attack on the d4 knight and goes for piece play instead of the compact set-up. It leaves the pin on f6 unanswered: White can capture there and damage Black's pawns, and keeps a slight edge.
Black builds a solid centre, guarding d5 and keeping the central break ...d5 in reserve. White's f-pawn advance has loosened the king's diagonal, which gives Black ideas of queen counterplay.

Meets the f-pawn advance in the centre: the pawn attacks the d4 knight and the f4 pawn at once, so White must resolve the tension. Black gets the Najdorf structure with a backward d6 pawn and a weak d5 square, in return for firm central space.

Answers the advance with a fianchetto, which gives a safe kingside pawn structure and a bishop on the long diagonal. Black aims for counterplay on the g1-a7 diagonal, where White's king would like to castle.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Venice Attack
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Punishes the immediate ...e5: with the a-pawn still on a7, Black cannot prevent the check and must block it. The usual blocks leave White's knight on f5, where it is hard to dislodge without concessions.
Retreats the knight to safety and avoids the awkward squares around b5, accepting a slower game. White keeps a pull on d5, since Black's pawns on e5 and d6 leave that square weak.
Jumps to f5 straight away, hitting d6 and g7. Without the preliminary check, though, Black frees the game with ...d5, which attacks e4 and opens the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Dragon Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: The main move: White prepares to castle long and storm the kingside with pawns, while Black's fianchettoed bishop and the half-open c-file bring counterplay on the other wing. It is the sharpest way to face the Dragon, and a slip by either side is punished quickly.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Dragon Variation, Classical Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..background: The oldest White response to the Dragon, and the second most common after the Yugoslav Attack.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: The calmer way: White prepares to castle short and plays for a controlled positional game instead of a pawn storm. The attack is slower than with the main move, which lets Black's long-diagonal bishop work with fewer worries.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Dragon Variation, Fianchetto Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop and prepares to castle short, mirroring Black's set-up. It is solid but slow: the two bishops meet on the long diagonal and White gets little more than equality.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Dragon Variation, Levenfish Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..background: Named after the Russian grandmaster Grigory Levenfish, who recommended it in the 1937 Russian Chess Yearbook. It is not very common at the highest level today.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Takes space and prepares e5 to hit the f6 knight at once, so Black has to cover e5 with a developing knight move. It is a sharp, trappy try, but it commits the f-pawn early and is rarely seen at the top level.

The point of the whole set-up: the fianchettoed bishop eyes the long diagonal toward the centre and the queenside, and Black can castle at once. With White's bishop on e2 there is no quick pawn storm to fear, so Black can play for counterplay on the c-file.
Hits the d4 knight at once and brings out the second knight, so that the king's bishop and castling can follow. It keeps the usual Dragon plan of the long diagonal and the c-file.
Mixes the Najdorf pawn move with the fianchetto and prepares queenside expansion with ...b5. It spends a tempo on the flank before the king is safe, so White can develop and castle in peace.

Completes the Dragon set-up: the bishop on the long diagonal presses on the centre and the queenside, and Black can castle at once. Black accepts a race with attacks on opposite wings and relies on the c-file and the bishop for counterplay.
Develops with an attack on the d4 knight, so White must decide at once whether to trade or retreat. It leads to the same Dragon set-up by a different move order.

Keeps the Najdorf pawn move in hand beside the fianchetto, aiming at queenside expansion with ...b5. It costs a tempo on the flank while White builds the usual set-up for castling long and a pawn storm against the king.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Dragon Variation, Levenfish Variation, Main Line
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Guards the e5 square before the pawn arrives, so the advance no longer wins time against the f6 knight. Black develops with a purpose and gets a sound position; the fast e5 push is the point of White's last move, and this move takes its sting away.
The accurate reply: the knight attacks d4 and guards e5, so the pawn advance that gives f4 its point no longer wins time against the f6 knight. Black keeps a solid Dragon set-up with equal chances.

Stops a white piece from landing on b5 and builds a hybrid of the Dragon and the Najdorf. It spends a tempo on the flank, and White keeps the choice between pushing the e-pawn and bringing the knight back to f3.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Richter-Rauzer Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: The most common reply: the bishop threatens Bxf6 to damage Black's pawns, keeps d6 under pressure and rules out a Dragon-style fianchetto. White plans to castle long, and the usual result is a sharp game with kings on opposite wings.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Classical Variation, Sozin Attack
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..background: The Fischer-Sozin Attack, which castles kingside after 7.Bb3 a6, is named after Bobby Fischer and the Russian master Veniamin Sozin, who originated it in the 1930s.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Puts the bishop on its most aggressive square, pressing on f7 and demanding a direct answer. White commits to a fight for the initiative: sharp, heavily analysed play with an attack on the king against Black's counterplay in the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Classical Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..background: White's third most common sixth move against the Classical Variation.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: The quiet development: White prepares to castle short and keeps the pieces compact. It leaves Black free to pick the pawn structure, so the game is a positional struggle rather than a race of attacks.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Spielmann Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Retreats the knight from the d4 square, avoiding a trade on d4 and keeping more pieces on the board. It also blocks the f1-bishop, so White gets a compact but passive set-up that offers little chance of an early advantage.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Classical Variation, Fianchetto Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop for a slower positional game. It is sound but does not put the same questions to Black as the more active bishop moves, so Black reaches an easy position.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Sozin Attack, Leonhardt Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: The main reply: the pawn shuts the bishop's diagonal to f7 and covers d5. Black accepts a slightly cramped position for solidity, and the game goes into sharp theory where White attacks the king and Black counterattacks.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Classical Variation, Anti-Sozin Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..background: Pal Benko's move against the Sozin Attack.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Puts the queen on the g1-a7 diagonal, attacking the d4 knight and the b2 pawn, so White must settle the tension in the centre at once. It avoids the razor-sharp main lines for more positional play.

Fianchettoes the bishop and heads for a Dragon-like game, but leaves the c4-f7 diagonal open with no pawn shield on e6. It is playable, yet less precise than closing the diagonal, and it gives White an easy choice of attacking set-ups.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Boleslavsky Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Claims the centre and hits the d4 knight at once. The pawn on e5 is supported by d6, giving Black a sound but slightly passive structure with a hole on d5, which White can use as an outpost.
Heads for the fianchetto set-up against White's quiet bishop. With the bishop on e2 the sharpest pawn storm is less likely, and Black can castle and use the long diagonal for counterplay.

Simplifies by trading a pair of knights, which eases Black's position. But White recaptures with the queen, taking a central post with a lead in development, and Black has given up the knight that controlled d4 and e5.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Richter-Rauzer Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..background: Vsevolod Rauzer introduced the modern plan of Qd2 and long castling in the 1930s.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: The main line: the pawn supports d5 and prepares the bishop's development. If White takes on f6, Black usually recaptures with the g-pawn, accepting a damaged kingside for the two bishops and a central pawn majority.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Richter-Rauzer Variation, Modern Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Develops the bishop first, supporting the c6 knight so that White's knight exchange on c6 can be answered with the bishop. It is a flexible, solid move that waits to see how White proceeds.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Richter-Rauzer Variation, Dragon Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: The fianchetto is not playable here: Bxf6 usually leaves Black recapturing with the e-pawn, because the g-pawn has left, wrecking the kingside structure, and Ndb5 then puts the d6 pawn under pressure.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4 Nc6.strategy: Attacks the queen with a developing move, so White has to move it again. The early queen sortie costs a tempo, which is the standard way of answering it.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4 a6.strategy: Takes the b5 square from the bishop in advance, so the next ...Nc6 hits the queen with a tempo and White cannot answer with the pin. A flexible way to meet the early queen.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on e4 and leaves ...Nc6 for later. It gives White the extra option of 5.e5, hitting the knight, so Black has to be more careful than after the immediate knight move.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4 Nc6 5..strategy: Pins the knight to the king, so it can no longer take the queen. White then trades bishop for knight, hoping that a lead in development makes up for giving Black the bishop pair.
A quiet retreat to a central square from which the queen guards e4. White plans simple development, but the queen blocks the c1-bishop and the plan asks little of Black.

Retreats the queen to its starting square and admits that the sortie lost time, since Black developed a knight with a tempo. The position is sound and White keeps an intact pawn structure, but has no compensation for the lost time.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4 Nc6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Chekhover Variation, Zaitsev Defence
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4 Nc6 5..strategy: Answers the pin by putting the queen behind the knight, so that the queen can recapture on c6. But the queen blocks the c8-bishop, and the move is a step behind the more usual development of the bishop to d7.
Breaks the pin at once and invites the exchange on c6. Black recaptures with the bishop and keeps both bishops, while White's lead in development has to pay for the early queen.
Develops with an attack on e4 but leaves the pin in place. White can take on c6 with check, and Black recaptures with the b-pawn, which loosens the queenside for the sake of development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.dxc5.strategy: Takes the pawn at once, a sharp sidestep of the usual knight development. White's e4 pawn is loose, so Black regains the pawn immediately and play opens, with the c5 pawn adding pressure on d6.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.Nc3.strategy: Defends the attacked e4 pawn with a developing move and keeps the tension in the centre. After the exchange on d4, White has the better-developed pieces and Black the open c-file and a central pawn majority, the starting point of the main Open Sicilian games.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.Bd3.strategy: Defends e4 with the bishop and keeps the c-pawn free for a later c2-c4 that would clamp the d5 square. The bishop is less actively placed than a knight on c3, though, and Black can challenge the centre at once and gain space with ...e5 against the knight that recaptures on d4.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.Bb5+.strategy: Checks and offers to trade Black's light-squared bishop, but does nothing for the attacked e4 pawn, so White still has to spend a move on it. A sound sideline, but Black's block develops a piece at no cost.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.dxc5 Nxe4.name: Sicilian Defence: Modern Variations, Anti-Qxd4 Move Order Accepted
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.dxc5 Nxe4.strategy: Takes the e4 pawn at once instead of recapturing on c5, so the exchange of pawns is met by an exchange: the knight takes a central post, and when White wins back d6, Black recaptures. The result is an open position with no pawns left in the centre for White, and Black has little to fear.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.dxc5 Qa5+.strategy: Checks first and eyes the c5 pawn, so White has to spend a move before Black wins the pawn back, with the e4 pawn still under attack. A respected alternative to the knight capture: the price is an early queen sortie and a less simple position.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.dxc5 dxc5.strategy: Recaptures the pawn and allows the queen exchange, after which Black can no longer castle and the king is stuck in the centre. White's e4 pawn is still attacked, but the quiet game is less promising than the active replies.
